text: The word “recommendation” may be a bit too strong, but for those interested in the topics below, here are some papers and other resources that I have found particularly interesting or which I haven’t yet read but would like to. I have adopted the rating system used in skiing to indicate the level of approachability, with green circles being the most approachable, blue squares being more challenging, and black diamonds being the most advanced. If a resource does not have a rating, it is because it should be approachable to anyone. None of these recommendations should be considered as an endorsement of the paper or its conclusions, but rather as a recommendation to read it and form your own opinion. Though the recommendations lean more technical, I have tried to include a mix of papers of varying technical sophistication, so there should be something for everyone.

title: Shannon’s Demon, Made Exact (Part 1)
text:
If intuition is any guide, it shouldn’t be possible for a long-only portfolio to be profitable when each of its component assets is a major lemon, unless, of course, one is clairvoyant and can predict those fleeting moments when random chance will favor each asset. Yet, as I’ll demonstrate in this post, not only is it possible to do this without any clairvoyance whatsoever, but also an investor can (almost surely) guarantee an exponential amount of money in the long run from an appropriately constructed portfolio of such lemons. It turns out that information theory provides a lovely explanation for why this is possible. The culmination of this post is a simple, closed-form formula for the excess expected growth rate of a portfolio, which is expressed as the difference between two Kullback-Leibler divergences – this is why it is natural to measure the growth rate in bits.
